text: [clean] Rotate crops so that no family grows in the same patch year after year.
[clean] Cut back spent flower stalks so that the plant directs energy into new growth.
[clean] Choose disease-resistant varieties whenever the catalogue offers them, for crops potatoes that suffer from blight in humid summers.
[clean] Net the currant berry bushes before the fruit ripens, or the birds will strip them within days.
[clean] Plant garlic cloves pointed end up, a span apart in loose soil.
[clean] Let the soil dry slightly between irrigations so the roots grow deep and strong.
[cool] Before the sowing of spring, spread a layer of compost over every row and dig it lightly into the soil.
[cool] Train climbing beans up tall sturdy poles to save ground space.
[cool] Scatter grit or ash near young hostas to deter slugs and snails.
[cool] Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last expected frost of spring.
[cool] Choose disease-resistant varieties for crops that suffered blight in earlier seasons, and record how each variety performed.
[cool] Rake the plot to a fine tilth before sowing,, because small seeds germinate in rough, lumpy ground.
[examine] Mulch newly planted rows with fresh straw to hold moisture through dry spells.
[examine] Keep the soil around blueberries acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) with ericaceous compost and collected rain.
[examine] Lift dahlia tubers after the first frost and store them until spring.
[examine] Collect rainfall in barrels under every downpipe so the garden has a reserve for irrigation.
[examine] If aphids cluster on the shoot tips, rub them off gently before the colony spreads to other plants.
[examine] Ventilate the greenhouse on sunny mornings so humid air does not encourage mould.
[heat] Never dig heavy wet clay, because treading on it ruins the soil structure.
[heat] Turn the compost pile so it keeps breaking down.
[heat] Build a compost heap so that it decomposes.
[heat] Always label each row with the variety name and the sowing date.
[heat] Plant onion sets with the tips just showing.
[heat] Bud roses in midsummer when the bark lifts easily from the rootstock.
[put] Trim yew and privet hedges twice a year (late spring and late summer) to keep them dense.
[put] Grow tall crops on the north side of the plot so that nothing shades the shorter rows.
[put] Pinch off the lower leaves of young vines to improve the air flow.
[put] Stake tall flowers before storms arrive so that the stems do not snap in strong wind.
[put] Grow a succession of crops (spring onions, radishes, salad leaves, dwarf beans).
[put] If the leaves turn yellow, test the soil before adding more fertilizer to the patch.
[puttwo] Start by testing the soil pH and amending it carefully before sowing the first seeds.
[puttwo] Sketch the plot, marking where every crop family grew the previous year, so that brassicas never follow in the same patch.
[puttwo] Divide crowded clumps of perennials every three or four years in early autumn, replanting the vigorous outer pieces of each clump.
[puttwo] Plan the garden in a notebook so that nothing is forgotten when spring arrives.
[puttwo] Test drainage by digging a 30 cm hole in several spots and timing how long the hole needs to drain.
[puttwo] When sowing beans, set a few extra at the end of each row.
